subject: Questions re analytical Form Predictive Inference for noise-free prediction with GP

messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: Questions re analytical Form Predictive Inference for noise-free prediction with GP
parts:
Hi all,

I wonder if any have tried to use analytical form of the joint predictive inference for f* (i.e. noise-free) instead of y* (with noise/jitter)?

I am trying to implement the neural network kernel as per R&W (code below). With noisy inference, it seemed to work.

However, when I tried to switch into noise-free prediction, STAN would complain about cholesky_decompose (of y_tilde_cov, code below) failing.

Any thoughts would be very helpful!

Many thanks,

Andy


STAN code:
data {
  int N;

  vector[N] y;
  vector[N] x;
}

transformed data {
  vector[N] gp_mu;
  real  K_2_div_pi;
  vector[2]     x_nn[N];
  row_vector[2] x_nn_t_x_2[N];
 
  gp_mu      <- rep_vector(0, N);
  K_2_div_pi <- 2/pi();

  {
    for (n in 1:N) {
      x_nn[n][1]   <- 1;
      x_nn[n][2]   <- x[n];
      x_nn_t_x_2[n] <- (2 * x_nn[n])';
//'
    }
  }
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
  vector<lower=0>[2] nn_sigma_sq;
  vector[N] y_tilde_nn;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;

  sigma <- sqrt(sigma_sq);
}

model {
  matrix [N, N] L_K_sigma;
  matrix [N, N] K_nn;
  matrix [N, N] K_nn_sigma;
  matrix [N, N] K_sigma;

  // NN kernel
  {
    matrix [2, 2]   Sigma_nn;
    row_vector[2]   tmp_2_x_nn_t_Sigma_nn[N]; // 2 * x_nn[i]' * Sigma_nn
    vector[N]       tmp_nn_denom;               // 1 + 2 * x_nn[i]' * Sigma_nn * x_nn[i]

    Sigma_nn[1,1] <- nn_sigma_sq[1]; 
    Sigma_nn[2,2] <- nn_sigma_sq[2];
    Sigma_nn[2,1] <- 0;
    Sigma_nn[1,2] <- 0;

    // pre-compute 
    for (n in 1:N) {
      tmp_2_x_nn_t_Sigma_nn[n] <- x_nn_t_x_2[n] * Sigma_nn;
      tmp_nn_denom[n]          <- tmp_2_x_nn_t_Sigma_nn[n] * x_nn[n];
    }
    tmp_nn_denom <- 1 + tmp_nn_denom;   

    for (i in 1 : N) {
      for (j in i : N) {
    real x1;
    real x2;
    real k;
   
    x1 <- tmp_2_x_nn_t_Sigma_nn[i] * x_nn[j];
    x2 <- sqrt(tmp_nn_denom[i] * tmp_nn_denom[j]);
    k  <- K_2_div_pi * asin(x1/x2);
   
    K_nn [i, j] <- k;
    if (i != j) {
      K_nn [j, i] <- k;
    }
      }
    }

    K_nn_sigma <- K_nn;
    for (n in 1:N) {
      K_nn_sigma[n,n] <- K_nn_sigma[n,n] + sigma_sq;
    }
  }

  K_sigma   <- K_nn_sigma;
  L_K_sigma <- cholesky_decompose (K_sigma); 
  y ~ multi_normal_cholesky (gp_mu, L_K_sigma);


  {
    vector[N] y_tilde;
    matrix[N,N] K_t_div_K_sigma;
    vector[N] y_tilde_mu;
    matrix[N,N] y_tilde_cov;
    matrix[N,N] L_y_tilde_cov;
  
    K_t_div_K_sigma <- K_nn'/K_sigma;
//'
      y_tilde_mu  <- K_t_div_K_sigma*y;
    y_tilde_cov <- K_nn_sigma - K_t_div_K_sigma * K_nn;
//    y_tilde_cov <- K_nn - K_t_div_K_sigma * K_nn;
    L_y_tilde_cov <- cholesky_decompose(y_tilde_cov);

    y_tilde_nn ~ multi_normal_cholesky (y_tilde_mu, L_y_tilde_cov);
  }


  // prior
  nn_sigma_sq[1] ~ normal (8, 4);
  nn_sigma_sq[2] ~ normal (2.18, 0.15);

  sigma_sq   ~ normal (-1, 1);
}

Setting the noise to zero turns the statistical problem into a deterministic
inverse problem, but MCMC is a terrible root finder so you’ll get nothing
but problems.  

GPs with no observation noise, however, have deeper issues.  Even
in models without Gaussian uncertainties it is common to add some
diagonal jitter to avoid these kinds of numerical problems.

Andy, I experienced the same issue when I explored a latent noise-free GP (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/IfWZAUsg9ag/18ex-N5WAAAJ). As Michael says, adding some jitter on the diagonal seems to be the solution. Note that with very small amounts of jitter (ex. 1e-7) chains will take a long time to compute and have low ESS. 


--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
